Case Study · GoodFail · Self-initiated

GoodFail: a workout tracker with a focused UX

As a designer, I can now build functional apps and solve real problems myself, without the overhead a startup carries. When the focus stays on user experience instead of aggressive monetization, the product can solve the problem better. GoodFail is that idea in practice: a workout building and tracking app whose core logging mechanic pushes you to focus and perform at a higher level.

Context

Popular workout apps get in their own way.

I train regularly, and every workout app I tried got in my way. They buried the thing I needed, logging a set fast mid-workout, under feeds, badges, and upsell screens. The core features I wanted sat behind a subscription.

Problem

Workout apps are focusing on mass appeal and profit, not solving the problem.

Startups are great early on, when they get to focus on the problem they set out to solve. But as time goes on, their investors are looking for a return.

That dynamic tends to turn a good app's pursuit of solving user problems into a pursuit of profitability. As a result, you get:

  • Gimmicky growth features that crowd the app and distract from its core value
  • Inconvenient subscription paywalls
  • A one-size-fits-all experience built for mass appeal, which dilutes the UX
How to start

AI allows for a faster and more organic design process

Just a few years ago, I would have started with deep competitive research, a sitemap, an extensive exploration of style, and a rigid definition of product scope. But the rapid design → build → test → iterate cycle that AI makes possible justified a more fluid process, with minimal guesswork. I could start designing and building the core experience on day one, then refine and expand as needed.

Design System

A confident, high-contrast identity

To feel like a real product, GoodFail needed a distinct voice. I built a tight system: navy carries anything about workouts, red anything about exercises, and purple is reserved for effort and failure, the concepts the app is named after. League Gothic sets the display type; Inter carries the rest.

Navy #426E8F Workouts. Plans, structure, and primary UI.
Red #CF2A0F Exercises. Exercise counts, badges, and key accents.
Purple #6C5CE7 Reserved for RPE and failure. Effort, by design.
Cream #EEEEEE The calm canvas the whole product rests on.

The palette is as restrained as the product. Purple appears only where the app measures how hard a set was or whether you hit failure. That discipline keeps the interface legible at a glance, when you're mid-set and not looking closely.

Solution

Every screen earns its place

GoodFail opens on a purposeful home screen with two states: a clean starting point with no active plan, and a focused dashboard when a plan is running. The whole app is organized around reaching your next set fast.

Fast logging, with memory

The set-logging screen is the heart of the app, so it got the most attention. A slider records how a set felt, and the app shows what you lifted for that set last time. Achieving progressive overload in your training takes no mental math: see what you did last time, beat it, keep moving forward.

A library and a history

"My Workouts" splits into two views via a single toggle. Library holds your reusable workouts, showing how many times you've completed each and how many exercises it holds. History is a chronological journal of every session, with a quiet "edited" tag on any day you changed a workout on the fly, so your record stays honest.

Planning without friction

Creating a plan uses a calendar range picker: tap a start date, tap an end date, and the span fills in. Leave it open-ended for a plan that just runs. The timeframe updates live beneath the plan name, so the commitment stays visible.

Design to Build

Closing the gap between Figma and product

What sets this project apart is that I didn't stop at the mockup. I built it. Working from my Figma designs, I used an AI-assisted workflow to turn each screen into a functioning app, reading exact values back from Figma using the Figma Desktop Bridge plugin with Claude Code so the build matched the design pixel for pixel.

1
Design each screen and the system in Figma
2
Translate designs into a working app, screen by screen
3
Verify the build against the design, value by value
4
Test on a real phone, refine, repeat

This tight loop let me feel my decisions in the hand. Interactions that looked fine in Figma sometimes felt wrong under a real thumb, and I could fix them on the spot. That kind of iteration only happens when the designer can touch the code.

Where it is now

A web app first, so I can learn fast

Right now GoodFail lives as a web app, a deliberate choice for this stage. A web build lets me iterate in the real world, installing it on my phone, using it in actual workouts, and tightening interactions without app-store review slowing each change. It's the fastest loop between noticing something and fixing it.

The web app is a testbed. The plan is to rebuild GoodFail in React and launch it as a real app, positioned as designed: a streamlined tool built around accessible, low-friction UX, sold once for a fair price with no subscription. The web phase proves the product feels right before the native phase ships it.

Now: web app

Hard Problems

Where design decisions met real constraints

Building it surfaced problems a mockup never would. A few shaped the final product:

01

Giving a fast start without taking over

I first pictured GoodFail as barely a step above a paper notebook, with every exercise and workout built by the user. In practice, that put an hour of setup in front of your very first workout, which is a fast way to lose someone. Preloading a handful of common exercises gives new users a quick start, and a working example of how exercises and workouts fit together, without taking the control away.

02

Making the frame feel native on a phone

The app had to lock to the viewport so only intended areas scroll, and respect the notch and home-indicator safe areas. These details are invisible on desktop but essential to feeling like a real app.

03

Simple without feeling cheap

GoodFail was meant to feel modest but effective from the start, so I designed for the lowest cognitive load I could manage. In some places that restraint paid off; in others it landed too basic, even unserious. Tightening the design without sacrificing ease of use was something only real-world testing could settle, one day of iteration at a time.

The Roadmap

Three features I'm building next

01

Supersets

Working multiple movements back to back is a staple of serious training. GoodFail should treat a superset as a first-class part of building a workout, not a workaround.

02

Rest timer

Most lifters time their rest with the phone's clock app and a bit of guesswork. A built-in timer that starts the moment you finish a set makes that simpler, and keeps you in the app.

03

Shareable plans

What happens when your strongest friend wants to set you up with his program? Today you'd have to turn him down. Shareable plans let one person hand a full workout plan to another in a tap.

The North Star

An algorithm that coaches the Good Fail

Before I rebuild GoodFail natively in React, there's one milestone I want to reach first.

A true progressive-overload engine, grounded in training science. Using the RPE effort rating on each set alongside the weight and reps you log, the app should recommend whether to add reps or add weight next time, so every exercise drives toward quality muscular failure: the Good Fail it's named for.

Get that right, and GoodFail stops being a place to record your training and becomes something closer to a coach in your pocket.

The bigger picture

What happens to the app market when anyone can build?

GoodFail started as a personal fix, but the way I built it points at something larger. A few years ago, a designer with this idea had two options: convince engineers to build it, or learn to code and spend months alone. I did neither. I designed it and used AI to help me build a working product, quickly and largely by myself.

That shift matters. When the distance between having a problem and building the thing that solves it shortens so dramatically, the economics of software change with it.

The argument

Fewer problems will wait for a startup to solve them

Much of today's app market runs on a familiar pattern. A startup finds a common need, builds a solution, then gates the useful parts behind a subscription under pressure to grow. The user's problem becomes leverage: you pay to stop the app from withholding what you came for.

That leverage only exists because building was hard. Remove the barrier, and the pattern gets harder to sustain.

As AI-assisted building becomes normal, more people will make small solutions to their daily problems: a tracker, a planner, a tool shaped to exactly how one person works. These builds carry minimal overhead, with no funding round to service, no growth targets, no reason to hold a feature hostage. They can just do the thing well.

So what happens to the market? Apps won't disappear, but gating value behind a paywall gets harder to defend when a motivated person can build the un-gated version over a weekend. Software that earns its price by being good and honestly sold outlasts software that survives on friction and lock-in.

GoodFail is a small, concrete argument for that future: a well-designed tool, built with minimal overhead, that skips the subscription model because it doesn't need one. If one designer can make this, plenty more will. The open question is what the market looks like once they do.
